title: Match the Records Library terms to MikroORM concepts
description: Drag each Records Library role on the left to the MikroORM concept it stands in for on the right. Get all five matches correct.

pairs.definition: Identity Map — one canonical in-memory instance per primary key, per EntityManager fork

pairs.term: Librarian's notebook of corrections collected at the desk
pairs.definition: Unit of Work — pending changes accumulated until flush()

pairs.term: The closing-time walk to the storeroom
pairs.definition: flush() — one ordered transaction that writes every change in dependency order
A forked EntityManager — per-request isolation of managed entities

pairs.term: A catalogue card you can scribble on
pairs.definition: A managed entity — a plain object whose mutations the Unit of Work tracks

modelAnswer: Master catalogue is the Identity Map (PK-keyed, per-EM-fork). The librarian's notebook is the Unit of Work — changes are deferred until flush(). The closing walk is flush() itself: one transaction, dependency-ordered. The reading-room desk is a forked EM (one per HTTP request). The catalogue card is a managed entity instance — MikroORM tracks every property mutation on it without you calling .save().

title: Why DataMapper, not ActiveRecord?
description: Pick the single best reason MikroORM ships with DataMapper as its primary mode rather than ActiveRecord, then justify your pick in at least 25 words referencing what changes for unit tests.

widgetConfig.question: Why does MikroORM make DataMapper the default and treat ActiveRecord as opt-in?

options.label: DataMapper is measurably faster at the SQL level than ActiveRecord.
DataMapper keeps persistence out of the entity, so the entity stays a plain class with no DB import — testable in isolation.
DataMapper has nicer syntax for find() than ActiveRecord.
ActiveRecord was deprecated in TypeScript ORMs around 2020.

widgetConfig.rubric: Strong answers note that an ActiveRecord entity must import a connection/session to call .save() — which makes the entity un-instantiable in a unit test without a real or mocked DB. DataMapper entities are POJOs; the EntityManager owns persistence, so you can `new Book({ title: 'x' })` in a test that never opens a socket.

modelAnswer: The correct pick is `decoupling`. An ActiveRecord Book has `book.save()` — which requires Book to know about the DB session. That means every unit test that instantiates a Book is implicitly an integration test. DataMapper splits the model from the EntityManager: the entity stays a POJO, persistence lives in the EM, and unit tests run with zero database. The benefit is invisible on a 200-line side-project and obvious on a multi-team codebase like Fohlio.

title: Why is the Identity Map per-request, not global? (AI-resilient)
description:
Draft a 3-5 sentence answer explaining why a shared, global Identity Map would be catastrophic in a multi-request web server. Then test your answer: paste your draft into ChatGPT and ask it to improve it. Identify one thing ChatGPT added or changed that you agree with, and one thing it missed or got wrong. Submit: your original draft, the ChatGPT output, and your one-line verdict on each. (Hint: think about concurrent requests mutating the same in-memory Book instance, and what 'stale data' means when 50 HTTP handlers share one map.)

Metacognitive memo: What was hard to articulate? What would an AI summary of this lesson probably miss about why per-request isolation matters?
modelAnswer:
Key reasoning the answer must include:
1. Two concurrent requests could load the same entity id into the same JS object. Request A mutates it; flush from Request B now writes Request A's dirty data to the database under Request B's transaction — silent data corruption.
2. A global map never gets cleared: entities loaded six hours ago stay 'managed', occupying memory and presenting stale state to any handler that asks for them.
3. Per-request fork() gives each handler its own reading-room; the head librarian's master catalogue is the source of truth, but each patron's desk is private.
AI limitation: ChatGPT typically gives a technically correct but surface-level answer. It often misses the flush-ordering issue under concurrent mutations — that it is not just a memory leak but a correctness bug.
